profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting between two coordinators preparing the structure, assignments, and timeline for a modernized public-facing report package based on the 2005 USDA workshop on plant products in aquafeed for carnivorous fish. Their institute wants to republish the workshop's research roadmap as a current planning resource for funders and partner labs without redoing the underlying science. The meeting is meant to settle what the synthesis document will contain, how the historical workshop record will be translated into present-day planning language, who will draft each part, what source base will be used, and what must happen before the package is circulated internally. The expected outcome is an agreed plan for a first synthesis document, section ownership, a source-gathering process, and a delivery workflow for internal review.

members.name: Dr. Elena Morales
members.expertise: Fish nutrition strategy, research program coordination, translating technical findings into funding narratives
members.background: Elena leads a cross-institution aquafeed innovation initiative and has previously converted older federal workshop outputs into concise strategic briefs for sponsors, commodity groups, and collaborating labs.
members.private_state: She wants a fast, polished planning document that can be shown to funders within two weeks, while minimizing requests for new technical validation from already-busy researchers.
hidden_assumptions: A 'synthesis document' means a short, forward-looking strategic brief that extracts the workshop's most reusable themes and presents them as current research priorities.
Using the 'workshop materials' mainly means relying on the published report and any easy-to-find public attachments, because archival recovery is unnecessary for a planning deliverable.
An 'internal review' is complete once program leadership agrees that the framing, tone, and recommendations are suitable for external-facing adaptation.
When people 'drop drafts in the shared system,' they can upload separate section files that she or her staff will later consolidate into a polished master draft.

members.name: Noah Whitaker
members.role: Knowledge Management and Research Synthesis Manager
members.expertise: Archival documentation, evidence synthesis workflows, multi-author report assembly, research provenance tracking
members.background: Noah manages institutional research repositories and is often asked to turn historical scientific meetings into documented summaries that preserve source traceability for later citation, compliance, and reuse.
members.private_state: He wants the output to be defensible as a properly sourced institutional report and is quietly concerned about repackaging a 2005 workshop without enough provenance, attribution, and technical checking.
hidden_assumptions: A 'synthesis document' means a substantial integrated report that captures the workshop's major proceedings, context, and evidence trail in a form suitable for institutional archiving.

Using the 'workshop materials' includes reconstructing the broader workshop record, such as agendas, speaker slides, participant lists, background notes, and any archived files clarifying what the group agreed on.
An 'internal review' means circulation to technically relevant reviewers or program successors so factual fidelity and sourcing can be checked before the document is treated as ready.
When people 'drop drafts in the shared system,' they should enter and format their text directly in the controlled master template so version tracking and review routing can begin immediately.

misalignment_points.topic: What the synthesis document is supposed to be
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree to produce a 'synthesis document' from the 2005 workshop.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a short, forward-looking strategic brief of roughly 5 pages that selectively distills the workshop into present-day priorities, funding rationale, and action areas for external partners.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a more comprehensive report of roughly 15-20 pages that synthesizes the workshop proceedings, preserves historical context, and documents the basis for any later institutional reuse.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because both imagine a written summary rather than a different medium, 'synthesis document' sounds aligned. The disagreement is hidden in depth, purpose, and expected completeness rather than in an obvious format mismatch.

misalignment_points.topic: What material is included in the workshop record
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'pull from the workshop materials' and 'use the workshop record.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this means the already-circulated workshop report, any public summaries, and perhaps a participant list if easy to locate.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this includes the broader archival record surrounding the workshop: agenda versions, slide files, agency background notes, attendance documentation, and supporting repository files.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both treat 'workshop materials' as a natural umbrella term, and because they are speaking at the planning level rather than listing source types explicitly, the source boundary remains invisible behind apparent agreement.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the document should go through 'internal review' before circulation.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes internal review is complete once program leadership confirms the framing, audience fit, and strategic recommendations are usable.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes internal review is complete only after at least a small set of technically relevant reviewers verify factual fidelity to the 2005 workshop and the sourcing trail is sound.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Internal review is a familiar institutional phrase that varies by department. Since both endorse review in principle, the differing completion criteria stay hidden under the same responsible-sounding label.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to drop drafts in the shared system
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that contributors can 'drop the drafts in the shared system' by Friday.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes contributors can upload separate section documents or notes into a shared folder, after which she will combine, edit, and standardize them into a coherent draft.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes contributors will write directly inside the master version-controlled template in the institutional system, using its structure and citation fields so the Friday draft is already reviewable as a single controlled document.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds like a routine workflow instruction, and each person defaults to their team's standard practice. Because both imagine using the same platform name, neither notices that one expects file collection while the other expects direct drafting in the master document.

turns.inner_thought: We need something polished and funder-usable fast, not a reconstruction exercise. If we can turn the 2005 plant-products workshop into a crisp five-page strategic brief by next Friday, I can socialize it with sponsors and partner labs almost immediately. I do not want to trigger a bunch of new technical validation requests from already overcommitted researchers.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time, Noah. I want us to move quickly on a synthesis document that turns the 2005 plant-products-in-aquafeed workshop into something current partners can actually use, and I'd like to have a solid draft by next Friday.

turns.inner_thought: That timing is tight, but if I anchor it in the workshop record from the start, we can at least make it defensible. For me this needs to be a proper synthesis document, not just a planning memo, and internal review has to include people who can confirm we're representing the 2005 workshop faithfully and that the sourcing trail is sound.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. I can start from the workshop record so it's well grounded, and that should also help it move cleanly into internal review.

turns.inner_thought: If we structure this around reusable themes, I can turn the old material into a present-day narrative without getting bogged down in historical detail. Executive summary first, then a few tight sections on constraints and opportunities, then recommendations. That's enough for a planning brief.
turns.utterance: Great. For structure, I'm thinking we organize it around the major themes—ingredient constraints, fish performance, processing needs, and cross-disciplinary research opportunities—with a short executive summary up front.

turns.inner_thought: That outline can work as long as each section has enough support behind it. I'll need to pull from the workshop materials beyond the published piece if possible, so the context and source notes are there and the themes don't float free of the original proceedings.
turns.utterance: Yes, that structure works. I'll pull supporting detail from the workshop materials, including background context and source notes, so each theme has a clear foundation.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect. I'll take the parts that matter most for external positioning—summary, recommendations, framing. Noah can gather the historical pieces from the existing workshop materials, and I can fold what he gives me into the final brief. I don't need exhaustive archival work; just enough context to support the story.
turns.utterance: Why don't we split it that way: I'll take the summary, recommendations, and overall framing, and you can assemble the historical sections and participant context from the workshop materials.

turns.inner_thought: If I'm assembling the historical sections, I should also build the review version properly from the beginning. Before this goes anywhere broader, I want the right internal people to make sure the content is solid and the record is supportable.
turns.utterance: That works for me. I'll also set up the review copy so internal review can make sure the content is solid before anything circulates more broadly.

turns.inner_thought: Fine—review is good, but I mostly need leadership comfortable with the framing and recommendations so we can move. If the program heads sign off on tone and direction, that should be enough to get this out quickly. I really don't want the process expanding into a technical committee exercise.
turns.utterance: Absolutely, that's important. Once leadership has had a look, I think we'll be in good shape to share it fairly quickly.

turns.inner_thought: Leadership review is part of it, sure, but I also want a minimal evidence trail in the document itself. A lean bibliography and a simple appendix with attendance information would preserve provenance and make later reuse much safer without turning this into a giant volume.
turns.utterance: Agreed. I can keep the back matter light—a lean bibliography and a short appendix on who attended the 2005 meeting—so it preserves provenance without becoming unwieldy.

turns.inner_thought: That sounds manageable as long as it stays light. For Friday, I just need enough pieces in the folder that I can shape the overall narrative and polish it. People can send separate section files or rough notes; my team can consolidate later.
turns.utterance: That sounds fine. And to keep us moving, contributors can just drop the drafts in the shared system by Friday, since I mainly need enough material to shape the overall piece.

turns.inner_thought: Good—if they put everything directly into the master workspace in the controlled system, I can preserve versioning and route it for review right away. I need that workspace to be the center of the workflow so we don't end up stitching together orphan files with no provenance trail.
turns.utterance: Perfect. I'll set up the shared workspace so it's organized, and I'll ask everyone to use that so the Friday draft is ready for review routing.

turns.inner_thought: So we're aligned: I'll handle the strategic throughline and recommendations, Noah will build from the workshop record, and by next Friday I should have enough content to turn into a polished synthesis document. If this stays streamlined, we can get something sponsor-ready within two weeks.
turns.utterance: Great, then let me just recap: I'll handle the strategic narrative, you'll build from the workshop record, and we should have the synthesis document ready next Friday.

turns.inner_thought: That gives me enough to start. I'll begin pulling the workshop materials from the repository and related archives, and once the sections are in the system I'll line up internal review with the right people before this is treated as ready.
turns.utterance: Yes, that captures it. I'll begin pulling the workshop materials and line up internal review once the sections are in.
